title: How Contemporary Artists Hijacked Grand Theft Auto
summary: Re_Spawn 11 (Rollover), 2021 Mathew Zefeldt The Hole A man in a white tank top speeds down a palm-lined highway. He jumps from his car, mid-traffic, and yanks open the door of the car beside him. A woman screams and bolts out. He climbs in, calm, and weaves through traffic as police sirens wail behind him. If you've never taken part in a scene like this, you're in a shrinking segment of the population. On November 19th, Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI, 13 years after its predecessor, and by almost all measures it’s the most successful video game launch of all time. It follows Jason and Lucia, a couple trying to climb the criminal ranks in Leonida, the series’s take on Florida, and its Miami-esque capital, Vice City. Despite the long wait, it’s been received with near-universal admiration (it scored a staggering 99 on Metacritic, the reviews aggregator) and exorbitant commercial success: on launch day, its retail sales were estimated at $3.79 billion, a record for any entertainment medium. GTA VI has garnered praise for its strong emotional core and stunningly believable game world. Yet many of the game’s central features are recognizable from the rest of the franchise, which launched in 1997: an open-world sandbox format, with a satirical take on real-world capitalism. GTA gives its protagonists the license to stray far from the main story, whether that’s surviving a shootout with the cops across a highway, skydiving from a jet plane, or watching the sun rise across the city from a secluded mountaintop. Those features have made it an inspiring cultural artifact to artists who have used GTA as a studio, a found landscape, and a shared reference. GTA’s recognizable aesthetic For Berlin-based artist Cemile Sahin , that shared cultural understanding is the point. GTA, she said, is “not only a game anymore.” If people see one of its characters out of context, “everyone knows it’s from GTA.” Sahin draws on that familiarity in her film Road Runner (2025), where a third of the action takes place inside the game. The film, part of a solo show at Esther Schipper Berlin in early 2025, imagines a world overrun by killer drones that lock people in virtual prisons. The film’s female protagonist is on a mission to save her sister, which means obtaining a facial cream that makes you invisible to surveillance, from an arms dealer on the black market. ROAD RUNNER, 2025 Cemile Sahin Esther Schipper The dystopian, madcap mission seems like a sardonic nod to GTA’s cynical sense of humor, but Sahin drew mostly from the game’s look. To turn the real-world actor who stars in the rest of the film into a video game avatar, a 3D artist rebuilt the main character from photo scans, down to her nails, Lacoste tracksuit, and a pink Bentley car. “The aesthetic that GTA has is super nice,” she said. “Everything is still kind of normal in this world, even though it’s crazy.” For a sci-fi story, that mix kept things, in her words, “still realistic.” Painting the GTA aesthetic That closeness to normal life also fascinates painter Mathew Zefeldt . In fact, from 2018 to 2023, Zefeldt painted only from GTA V. Plenty of video games offer “a more obvious escapism,” he said, like in sci-fi or fantasy. GTA instead contains an “uncanny mirror-like quality of our world.” GTA V is set in Los Santos, a version of Los Angeles, and since Zefeldt grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area suburbs, the city felt familiar. “Me playing as my avatar, a version of me in a version of L.A., is super strange,” he said. “It’s a version of a self-portrait.” Many of his paintings are composite images, and often repeat the terrain of the GTA landscape in carefully replicated segments, like tiles. Though analog, they recall the glitchy aesthetic of much earlier video games like Doom (1993), where textures visibly repeat in blocks. It’s only when you look very closely that you’ll see the paint blobs and brush marks that distinguish one image from another. In his 2025 show “ Reflections ” at The Hole , for example, his acrylic paintings of CGI ivy and rock-filled landscapes are evidence of his obsession with replicating imagery. “The repetition in my paintings is exaggerating that gesture of constructing this world virtually,” the artist said. Tree and Fern , 2019 Mathew Zefeldt The Hole Elegy, 2022 Mathew Zefeldt The Hole Zefeldt took tens of thousands of GTA V screenshots on his PlayStation with one rule: no photo mode, only live gameplay. That meant, if he missed a shot, he had to make it happen again. That often meant “circling back and jumping my car off the cliff again,” he said. Evidence of those virtual stunts is visible in his work Elegy (2022), a four-way split canvas where each image shows a chrome sports coupe soaring through the sky. Reality vs game world The work was part of a 2023 show at The Hole, “ Re_spawn ,” in which the artist turned his own image into the material. He reworked his avatar to look as much like him as possible, and most of the paintings show some version of his reflection. The likeness ran both ways. He didn’t like the game's T-shirts, so he dressed his avatar in a polo shirt. “Because of that, I started wearing polo shirts in real [life],” he said. “I let my physical body be influenced by my digital avatar.” Perhaps thankfully, he doesn’t act like his virtual avatar. Because avatars can respawn after death, it can make a player “much more reckless with your body, with your automobile, with other people around you,” Zefeldt said. The NPCs (non-playable characters such as the bystanders you hit with your pickup truck as you swerve onto a sidewalk) “don’t feel things,” and nothing has real consequences, he said. Blending In, 2022 Mathew Zefeldt The Hole Surface Texture I, 2023 Mathew Zefeldt Moosey Breaking the game’s rules But NPCs in GTA aren’t the totally blank canvas they might seem. For their works, Alexandra Pfammatter and Marco de Mutiis, who work together as the artist duo 2girls1comp, dug into GTA V’s animation library, the file that lists every movement the game assigns to its NPCs. Those moves, they found, were determined not only by situation, but by “what class they belong to, what gender they have, or what race they are programmed to perform,” Pfammatter said. Most dance moves, for instance, were reserved for female-coded NPCs, many of them sex workers. By “modding” the game (the hugely popular practice of hacking video games to alter how they look or work), the pair produced the video work Dancing Plague (2024), which was on view earlier this year in “Gaming the Civic,” a program at Helsinki’s Art and Media Culture Agency. For this work, one key press forces every male NPC to drop whatever he’s doing and start “feverishly executing those dance moves.” Even pilots (in GTA V, they’re all male) abandon the controls, so planes fall from the sky. When life imitates games This work was presented during a performance from choreographer Nina Davies, who works from the other direction: real people moving like NPCs. Her film Precursing (2023), she said, was responding to social media—what she called “the TikTok trend of people moving like NPCs in real life.” Davies watches new dance trends closely and always asks the same question: “Why are people moving like this today?” Her video and performance work looks back on the NPC craze as if it were a form of traditional dance. Reality, however, always creeps in. In rehearsal, her dancers found GTA V’s movements too human to be distinguishable. They switched to the stiffer GTA: San Andreas (2004), where “the fingers don’t separate,” she explained. How GTA VI could shape art As the franchise becomes ever more realistic, it’s hard to imagine what Davies and other artists will make of GTA VI. The NPCs in the 2026 game interact with players like they have lives of their own . That’s just one part of the game’s Herculean effort to mirror reality and faithfully recreate every element of the Miami in 2026 that it’s based on (right down to the manatee mailboxes ). Zefeldt, for one, isn’t rushing to make art out of the new game. “Right now I don’t have specific plans. I’m sure some paintings will come out of it,” he said. Whatever he makes, it won’t be fan art. “The paintings reflect the video game. The video game reflects the world.” The real question, he said, is “what is Grand Theft Auto saying about our world?”

title: Artist Rachel Whiteread to design trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards.
summary: British artist Rachel Whiteread has been commissioned to design the trophy for the 2027 BRIT Awards, the annual awards for British and international music. The artist’s design will be presented to winners at the annual music awards ceremony, which will take place at Manchester’s Co-op Live arena on February 27, 2027. Whiteread follows a succession of prominent artists and designers who have reimagined the trophy, which takes its form from Britannia, the female personification of Britain. Previous designers include Tracey Emin , Peter Blake , Vivienne Westwood , Zaha Hadid , Rachel Jones , and Slawn . For her design, Whiteread has drawn on her signature artistic approach of making negative space visible. Throughout her career, the artist has used materials such as plaster, resin, and concrete to cast the spaces within and around everyday objects, from furniture to entire buildings. “I used the moti of the BRIT Award and tried to change it in some way,” Whiteread said in a statement. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music.” In 1993, Whiteread became the first woman to win the Turner Prize , the same year she unveiled House (1993), a life-sized concrete cast of the interior of a Victorian terraced house in East London. In 1997, she became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale in a solo presentation. Among her most significant public commissions is the Judenplatz Holocaust Memorial (2000) in Vienna, a concrete sculpture resembling an inverted library that commemorates the 65,000 Austrian Jews murdered in the Holocaust. She was awarded a damehood in 2019 for her services to art. “Art and culture are under very real threat, so I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists—whether from music or the visual arts,” Whiteread added. Last year’s trophy was designed by British fashion designer Matthew Williamson, and awards were won by musicians including Olivia Dean, Wolf Alice, and Sam Fender. The 2027 ceremony will be broadcast on ITV1 and ITVX in the U.K.

title: Hoor Al Qasimi will curate the 2028 Venice Biennale.
summary: Hoor Al Qasimi, president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, will curate the 2028 Venice Biennale, La Biennale di Venezia announced on Thursday. The board had appointed her on November 20 as director of the Visual Arts Department, after the biennale’s president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco recommended her. The 62nd International Art Exhibition will run from April 8 to November 26, 2028, with pre-opening days on April 5, 6, and 7. The title and theme of the exhibition are not yet announced. Al Qasimi will take on the show two years after the 2026 edition, whose curator, Koyo Kouoh, was announced in December 2024. Kouoh died in May 2025 , and the exhibition, " In Minor Keys ," went ahead as planned under the team she had assembled. Buttafuoco praised Al Qasimi's “rare ability to listen to places and their people.” He linked her “balance and composure” to mīzān, or inner harmony. “We entrust her with the 62nd International Art Exhibition with great confidence,” he said. Al Qasimi said she first visited the Biennale's 50th edition in 2003, soon after she began curating the Sharjah Biennial, and called Venice “a critical space” for engaging with artists and curators. “I am honoured to have been invited to curate this exhibition,” she said, and thanked the board and Buttafuoco for their trust. She has run the Sharjah Biennial since 2003 and founded the Sharjah Art Foundation in 2009. In 2023, she curated the biennial’s 15th edition , a show Okwui Enwezor conceived before his death in 2019. She was artistic director of the 2025 Aichi Triennale in Japan, the first curator from outside the country to lead it, and curated the 2026 Biennale of Sydney. She also curated the United Arab Emirates pavilion at the 2015 Venice Biennale. ArtReview named her the most influential person in the art world on its 2024 Power 100 list , up from 36th place the year before. In 2025, she ranked third .

title: 5 Artists on Our Radar This November
summary: Volcano, 2026 Nooka Shepherd Soho Revue Mai, 2026 Rogé Girard Galerie C.O.A “Artists on Our Radar” is a monthly series focused on five artists who have our attention. Utilizing our art expertise and Artsy data, we’ve determined which artists made an impact this past month through new gallery representation, exhibitions, auctions, art fairs, or fresh works on Artsy. Chidy Wayne B. 1981, Castellón, Spain. Lives and works in Barcelona. Man In the Mirror III, 2026 Chidy Wayne Southern Guild Pugnator 109, 2026 Chidy Wayne Southern Guild Spanish Guinean artist Chidy Wayne makes works that feel ancient and contemporary at once, with motifs that draw from both his European and African ancestry. Over the years, Wayne has defined his own lexicon of archetypal imagery—cartoonish depictions of chubby hands, realistic men’s heads painted onto paper-doll-like bodies—which he renders in a limited earth-tone palette across painting, drawing, and textiles. Wayne worked as a fashion designer and a commercial illustrator before committing himself fully to art in 2017. In those careers, he spent countless hours drawing by hand—a dexterity evident in his confident works. Today, Wayne often begins a painting with his nondominant hand, or with his eyes closed, to capture a sense of what he considers “honest feeling” in his works. His most recent paintings are currently on view at his solo show “ Monomyths ,” at Southern Guild ’s New York location through January 9, 2027. These layer oil, charcoal, sand, sawdust, and plaster on canvas or jute. These works sometimes feature his family members, including his father, considering the similarities we inherit from our family. It’s part of a significant run of shows in recent years. In 2024, Grège Gallery in Bruges, Belgium, presented his solo show “ Echoes of the Self .” The following year he opened the solo exhibition “ Ancestral Futures ” at Francis Gallery in Los Angeles. This year, Southern Guild has presented Wayne’s works at Frieze Los Angeles, Frieze New York, the Aspen Art Fair, and Frieze London. Nooka Shepherd B. 1998, London, U.K. Lives and works in the West Country, England. Eve Giving Birth To Herself, 2025 Nooka Shepherd Soho Revue Goblin Pulp And Goblin Dew, 2025 Nooka Shepherd Soho Revue English artist Nooka Shepherd ’s paintings and drawings are filled with chimerical feminine beings. In the painting Eve Giving Birth to Herself (2025), for instance, a crouched nude woman raises up her arms in a gesture of exaltation, while a serpent emerges from her genitalia and circles her. The snake’s hissing red tongue becomes a kind of external circulatory system for the figure and a red orb, reminiscent of the biblical forbidden fruit, hovers overhead, with an embryo shown growing inside. In other works, women emerge from botanical forms or appear as sphinxes. Shepherd paints in a carnivalesque palette of icy pinks and blues alongside saturated reds, yellows, and blacks, and their figures have powder-white faces and rouged cheeks, heightening the sense of spectacle in the works. The artist’s inspirations include regional folklore and mythology and Shepherd has said their works are a way of connecting to the ancient and natural world through femininity, matrilineal ancestry, and fertility. Their works are currently on view in “ Feast of Saturnalia, ” a group show at London’s Soho Revue examining symbols of transition and impermanence. In 2025, their solo show “ House on the Borderland ,” also at Soho Revue, brought together paintings and ceramics that tapped into the artist’s memories of childhood through landscape. Shepherd earned a BFA from the Slade School of Fine Art in 2020, after winning the Thomas Epsley Painting Prize in 2017. In 2024, the artist was included in the group exhibition “ The Witch Burns ” at TIN MAN ART followed by the solo exhibition “ Grass Stained Heart ” at Soho Revue. Juliano Mazzuchini B. 1981, Jacareí, Brazil. Lives and works in São Paulo. Banheiro, 2026 Juliano Mazzuchini Marlyn Gallery Mesa Amarela, 2026 Juliano Mazzuchini Marlyn Gallery Brazilian artist Juliano Mazzuchini began his career as a theater actor, training at the Escola Livre de Teatro de Santo André in Brazil. In 2017, he transitioned to full-time painting, but the power of gesture and the body, integral to his work on the stage, remain at the core of his paintings. Mazzuchini creates gestural, often starkly lit scenes, where figures seem to be facing down a spotlight. In one work, Banheiro (2026), a woman clad in a white nightgown leans against a bathroom wall, her face seemingly obliterated by the brightness of the light. In other paintings, farm animals appear running through domestic space. In Mesa Amarela (2026), a horse trots through the doorway into a cramped kitchen like something from a Surrealist film. Other times, he paints three-quarter portraits (including one of the artist David Hockney ), which he blurs and smears, in a manner that is reminiscent of Lucian Freud . Mazzuchini is self-taught as a painter. In 2023, he opened a solo exhibition at Martha Pagy Escritório de Arte in Rio de Janeiro. His work has also been shown in Argentina, France, and the U.S., at venues including Galerie 20 Thorigny in Paris, Proa21, and MACBA in Buenos Aires. In 2024, he was shortlisted for The Hopper Prize. Lindsay Merrill B. 1987, Redwood City, California. Lives and works in Philadelphia and West Virginia. Stag, 2026 Lindsay Merrill Enari Gallery Head on wall I, 2026 Lindsay Merrill Enari Gallery Domestic space becomes uncanny and cinematic in American artist Lindsay Merrill ’s oil on canvas paintings. The artist mines the idiosyncrasies of rural and suburban American life, painting taxidermy, molded plastic Christmas lawn ornaments, rural storefronts, and other uncanny but everyday subject matter. These paintings become cinematic, even eerie, through her stark use of light and shadow. Taxidermy animal heads hang on a paneled wall in one work, while in others, the deer seem to have regained their sentience, and appear seated peacefully on arm chairs or unmade beds. Merrill has described her paintings as a way of reckoning with the American spirit and the values and environments that shaped her. Merrill received a BFA from Carnegie Mellon University and a master’s of Social Work from the University of Denver. In 2024, her works were included in group shows at Enari Gallery and Fortnight Institute, as well as in a solo show “Moving Targets” at Solito Gallery . Currently, her works are on view in two concurrent solo exhibitions “ Daughter ” at Enari Gallery (through December 20th) and “Ghosttown” at Rolando Anselmi (through December 12th). Her painting Daughter was recently acquired by the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City. Rogé Girard B. 1972, Saint-Hyacinthe, Canada. Lives and works in Montréal. Kawawachikamach, 2026 Rogé Girard Galerie C.O.A Wapizagonke, 2026 Rogé Girard Galerie C.O.A Montréal-based painter Rogé Girard paints vibrant semi-abstract landscapes in acrylic on canvas. He builds his scenes through a layering of gestures and forms that teeter on the edge of legibility without ever fully resolving. His newest paintings take their names from the varied terrains of Quebec province and he hints at these landscapes within their forms. In the painting Kawawachikamach (2026), squiggles and dashes of blues, purples, and blacks suggest a moonlit wood with a hill rising from a lake. Earlier this fall, the artist opened a solo exhibition, “ Échouerie ,” at Galerie C.O.A in Montréal. His works were also included in the group show “ Assembly ” at TAPPAN in Los Angeles. In addition to his career as an artist, Girard is an acclaimed book illustrator. He has twice been awarded Canada’s Governor General’s Award, and his book Haiti My Country earned recognition from the New York Times .

title: Naudline Pierre Draws on Her Caribbean Ancestry in Mystical Paintings of Nymphs
summary: Naudline Pierre is painting an altar to the elements. The contemporary artist, best known for her dreamy paintings of celestial beings with long tresses, was putting the final touches on a six-canvas polyptych, titled Sky, Earth, Sea (all works 2026), during a recent visit to her studio in Brooklyn. When installed, the paintings will form a vertical column topped by an arched canvas and will tower nearly 40 feet tall. The work is an ascent through the elements, with the canvases at the bottom depicting the sea, followed by the earth in the middle, and culminating with the heavens in the top three canvases. “When you’re in school as a kid, you learn the atmosphere and its different breakdowns,” Pierre said. “I was thinking about making a cross section of these worlds that I’m interested in.” Commissioned by the ICA Miami , the work is set to be unveiled just as Miami Art Week kicks off, installed in the museum’s three-story stairwell. It’s Pierre’s most ambitious installation to date. Now represented by Norr Cohan, Pierre earned an MFA in painting from the New York Academy of Art in 2017. Later that year, she had her breakout debut solo show, “Visitors,” at Thierry Goldberg in New York. Her work is currently the subject of a solo museum show, “May the Light Reach You,” at the Akron Art Museum, and was recently included in the group exhibition “House of Nisaba” at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, which closed earlier this year. Sky, Earth, Sea is her first museum commission, however. For the occasion, Pierre pushed her amorphous worlds in more narrative and compositionally complex directions as she considered ways to work within the long space of the ICA’s stairwell. The rise of Pierre’s mythic world Pierre has been painting her sumptuous mythical worlds for close to a decade. She populates her often jewel-toned scenes with female beings who are at once angelic and sprightly, fantastic and fickle. “They don’t have to be defined,” she said of these beings. “They’re beautiful when they’re angry. They’re beautiful when they’re in love. They’re beautiful when they’re bratty.” Celestial beings have filled Pierre’s paintings in some form since the start. At first, a single protagonist, an avatar or even an alter ego, moved among protective winged seraphim. Eventually, this single figure vanished and her attendants took over, multiplying into a pantheon. The artist, who was born in Massachusetts to Haitian parents, was raised in a devoutly religious household, and her artworks tap into aspects of these traditions. In the case of Sky, Earth, Sea , the installation takes inspiration from polyptych altarpieces. Even working at this scale, Pierre keeps her process intuitive; she needs to soak up the world before she can wring imagery from herself. “I feel like I’m always working on everything, even though it’s not a physical thing,” she said, “It’s a mental boiling down of things.” That means long stretches of sitting, staring, and flipping through art books before she touches the canvas. “Once I figure something out, I’m over it,” she said. “I want to be in the dark too. Leaving that space open for mystery and for me not knowing what it’s going to look like really helps because it doesn’t lock me into an idea.” Naudline Pierre’s inspirations While Pierre’s beings have long floated and danced through undefined space, in Sky, Earth, Sea she brings them into narrative spaces. “I think I’ve really expanded my color palette and my sense of space,” she said. “I wanted to take up the museum space and overwhelm the senses.” Pierre is an art history enthusiast, with books piled on every surface of her studio, including tomes covering everything from the Romantic era to the Surrealists . El Greco , in particular, has been a touchstone as she situates her figures in more concrete spaces. “I’m always looking at the Italian Renaissance as well as El Greco and William Blake . These are the same artists I’ve been looking at forever,” she said. “I’m a creature of habit.” In the painting Languid Grotto , the canvas that transitions from the oceanic realm to the terrestrial, sea nymphs languish on rocky crags on either side of a waterfall. In composing the work, Pierre considered how El Greco would have approached such terrain. Canvas shows through in dry, brushy passages that echo the Spanish master’s compositions. In place of the jewel tones she’s well known for, Sky, Earth, Sea embraces a palette of pastels (pale pinks, sea greens, and baby blues) reminiscent of the Rococo era. This transition started with Pierre incorporating a cotton-candy blue paint that she adopted to challenge herself. “I thought: What if the sky was blue? Whereas in my previous work, the sky could be hot pink. It could be green, it could be purple,” she said. She thinks of these paintings as embracing a kind of Romanticism . This melding of references is intrinsic to Pierre’s process. “I’m out there picking and choosing what I want to use and combining it to make something I want to see.” A love letter to Miami and the sea nymphs of the Caribbean Miami was top of mind for Pierre as she painted Sky, Earth, Sea . She lived in the city for a couple of years after college, before moving to New York, and her parents still live there. “I have a lot of love for the city and for the vibes and for all of the different cultures represented in Miami,” she said. For Pierre, incorporating a bathing scene of sea nymphs between the heavenly realms at the top of the installation and the oceanic scene at the base became a way to engage with one of the most ubiquitous motifs in art history and with her own Caribbean heritage. Years ago, Pierre took a trip to the Cayman Islands and recalled swimming in the ocean there as a near-spiritual experience. “I’d been thinking about my Caribbean ancestry relating to water,” she said. In creating the installation, she thought about Miami and the feeling of being in warm water and then in the warm air of a tropical environment, ascending from the sea to the tempestuous skies and storms of the region. The top three canvases, Mythic Heavens , Aerial , and the crowning arched canvas Aerosphere , are filled with pink angels soaring amid dark, Romantic clouds. The angels use the clouds as a platform, a stage. “These nymphs are at leisure, and the celestial beings are dancing or they’re kind of lounging. It’s just about existing,” Pierre said. Following this monumental endeavor, Pierre hopes to return to jewel-like, small-scale paneled works and altarpieces. “I love the extremes, really, really big or really, really small,” she said. “The middle is kind of boring for me.” As for what comes next, Pierre is still dreaming, “There’s always a new corner for me to discover.…Maybe it’ll be in space.”

title: Gallerist Rajiv Menon Wants South Asian Artists to Become Household Names
summary: When you meet Rajiv Menon, he is likely smiling. His hair is brushed back in gentle curls, his feet tapping, as though he is already on his way somewhere. The Los Angeles–based gallerist and founder of Rajiv Menon Contemporary seems to have inherited this restless energy. “My father was in the merchant navy, and my parents spent the first two years of their marriage at sea,” he told Artsy. “I guess that is where my primordial urge to move and connect between cultures comes from.” That impulse now shapes his approach to running the gallery he founded in 2023 to champion South Asian and diasporic artists. At a moment when art from the region is attracting greater international attention, Menon has emerged as one of its most energetic advocates. His ambitious programming and spirited appearances on the international art circuit have quickly made him one of the most talked-about young gallerists in the industry . Growing up between worlds Menon’s own journey began in Houston, where he grew up with immigrant parents originally from Kerala in South India. “While Houston was a cosmopolitan city, we lived in the suburbs, which could feel less welcoming,” he noted. Menon remembers his parents turning down Indian music in the car whenever other people were around, afraid of drawing attention to themselves. Summer visits to see family in India, on the other hand, revealed another, more expressive version of his parents, at ease in the country they had left behind. In high school, Menon discovered the writer Jhumpa Lahiri, and with her, a language for the peculiar loneliness of growing up between cultures. First came Interpreter of Maladies , followed by The Namesake , a novel he still rereads every few years. In Lahiri’s stories of immigrant families, grief and displacement, he felt a familiarity. “The depiction of grief really hit me at my core,” he recalled. “It made me feel less alone.” Here was the extraordinary power of art: to make a singular experience feel universal. “It was an instant recognition that I wanted to dedicate my life to culture.” Making space for South Asian art Menon studied international affairs and English, followed by a PhD at New York University, where his research examined representations of masculinity across Indian cinema, American television, and contemporary art. Outside the classroom, New York offered another education. “I loved the spontaneity of stumbling into galleries,” he said. Museums, film festivals, and exhibitions became his extended syllabus. Eventually, he grew restless with studying culture from a distance. He wanted to participate in its making and took a job in advertising and market research, followed by a career in television production that brought him to Los Angeles. It was a time when streaming platforms were taking off, opening doors for new voices and stories. Yet Menon grew disillusioned with Hollywood’s conversations around South Asian representation: “It felt very shallow,” he recalled. After nearly a decade in entertainment, he found himself longing for the intellectual rigor of his academic years. Art offered a meeting point between the two worlds. He had begun collecting, making studio visits and obsessively discovering artists such as Hiba Schahbaz , Asif Hoque , Anoushka Mirchandani , Bhasha Chakrabarti , and Sanié Bokhari with such enthusiasm that friends assumed he was already in the business. That summer, wandering through galleries in London, he realized something was missing back home. Los Angeles, despite its cultural diversity, had few commercial spaces dedicated to contemporary South Asian art. “I wanted to create something I wasn’t seeing in Los Angeles: a gallery that really prioritized South Asian culture,” he said. Menon trialed the idea with a series of temporary pop-up exhibitions around town before settling into its permanent home on Highland Avenue in February 2025. Its inaugural exhibition, “EXHIBITIONISM,” brought together 19 South Asian and diasporic artists, including Chitra Ganesh , Sunil Gupta , Shyama Golden , and Raghav Babbar , to explore themes of privacy, intimacy, and the desire to be seen. The show was something of a mission statement for Menon, and the timing of his project is fitting. New York, where he studied, now has Zohran Mamdani, the son of Indian-origin parents, as mayor. Los Angeles, his adopted home, has just elected India-born Nithya Raman as its first South Asian mayor. In two of the U.S. cities that shaped his life, the public face of South Asian identity is changing. Taking South Asian art beyond borders “I dream of a world where South Asian artists are household names,” said Menon, who notes that recognition is just the start. He wants South Asian artists to be understood not simply for where they come from, but for the ideas and questions their work brings to the world. “Specificity becomes a road to universality,” he says, drawing on philosopher Kwame Anthony Appiah’s idea of “rooted cosmopolitanism”: that one can belong deeply to a place while remaining open to the world. The gallery’s program has followed this thinking across borders. In 2025, Menon curated “Non-Residency” at Jaipur’s City Palace in Rajasthan, India, bringing diasporic artists into conversation with India. In 2026 came Chandigarh-based Gurjeet Singh ’s first solo exhibition outside India and Babbar’s U.S. solo debut, presented in Los Angeles and New York’s Armory Show, respectively. At Art Mumbai, the gallery’s “West Coast” presentation reversed the journey, introducing Los Angeles–based artists to Indian audiences. Other ventures have taken Menon further beyond his gallery space, from curating “Time Pass” at New York’s Half Gallery to a print exhibition at London’s The Permit Room restaurant and its lodgings. The gallery has also helped place works in major American museum collections including the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco and ICA Miami. But for all the attention paid to museums and collectors, Menon seems equally interested in what happens when someone wanders into his gallery off the street. His lively, often impromptu walkthroughs have become something of a signature. Whenever he is there, he likes to lead them himself, slipping between art history, personal anecdotes, and unexpected connections, with the enthusiasm of a student who has never stopped learning. The pleasure, for him, seems to lie as much in the questions as in the answers. “Art is for everybody, whether you can buy it or not,” he said. Perhaps this is what Menon has been building all along. Not simply a gallery for South Asian art, but a place where strangers might recognize themselves in other people’s stories. Much as he did, years ago, reading Lahiri in suburban Texas.

title: All the Art You Need to See during Miami Art Week 2026
summary: The first week of December means one thing in the American art world: Miami! Every year, the city hosts a somewhat frenzied week of art fairs, exhibitions, parties, and many, many events, all centered on Art Basel Miami Beach. And it’s not just the art crowd driving the action. Brands across industries descend on the city, too. This year, for example, LEGO is teaming up with Derrick Adams on an interactive sculpture project, Pantone is throwing a party for its color of the year, and Miele and Elle Decor are bringing a “sensory kitchen installation” to the Miami Beach Botanical Garden. Amid all the activity, there’s a wealth of art to see. Here’s our 10-stop guide to making the most of Miami Art Week 2026. To build your own art-filled itinerary, check out City Guide in the Artsy app , where you can discover and save the shows, fairs, and galleries you want to visit. 1. Art Basel Miami Beach Dec. 2–6 | Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Dr. | Miami Beach Miami Art Week wouldn’t be the same without its centerpiece, Art Basel Miami Beach , which returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center for its 24th edition. This year, its more than 270 exhibitors span major international galleries, mid-size dealers, and emerging names. The fair opens with VIP previews December 2nd and 3rd, followed by public days December 4th–6th. While there, don’t miss Zero 10, Art Basel’s section dedicated to art of the digital era, returning to Miami Beach for its second and largest edition yet. Among the highlights are DRIFT ’s Murmuring Minds (2024), an installation of robots that respond to visitors’ movements, presented by TAEX , and lauded AI artist Refik Anadol ’s collaboration with the Yawanawá people of the Amazon. 2. Untitled Art, Miami Beach Dec. 1–6 | Ocean Drive and 12th St. | Miami Beach One of the pleasures of Miami Art Week is stepping out of an art fair and straight onto the beach. Now in its 15th edition, Untitled Art, Miami Beach returns to its oceanfront tent, bringing together contemporary galleries from around the world. The Nest section, dedicated to emerging galleries, is always an exciting place to discover new names. The fair opens with a VIP and press preview on December 1st, followed by public days December 2nd–6th. This year’s Special Projects, curated by Damîen Dakota, explore the theme of cognitive dissonance. Works in the program include Gabo Arora’s AI-powered The Great Dictator (2026), Germane Barnes ’s Pull Up a Chair (2026), and Signe Pierce ’s ELECTROTEXTURE (2014–present). Also happening at Untitled Art this year is Artnet Airwaves , Artnet’s new live podcast festival, taking place December 2nd and 3rd. The program features five live recordings, including Artnet’s The Art Angle and Art Market Minute , alongside Bad at Sports , Nota Bene , and NewCrits . 3. NADA Miami Dec. 1–5 | Ice Palace Studios, 1400 N. Miami Ave. | Downtown Miami If you’re looking to discover new artists, NADA Miami should be high on your list. The fair’s 24th edition brings together more than 130 galleries and art spaces from 27 countries, including 45 first-time exhibitors. NADA is consistently one of the best places to encounter emerging talent and galleries you may not know. The fair holds an invitation-only preview on December 1st at 2 p.m., followed by public admission starting at 4 p.m. and running through December 5th. 4. Design Miami Dec. 1–6 | Convention Center Dr. and 19th St. | Miami Beach Resin Console, 2026 Chris Schanck David Klein Gallery Just across the street from Art Basel, Design Miami is an annual favorite where the line between functional objects and art becomes wonderfully blurred. Curated by Charlene Prempeh, this year’s edition takes “Unveiling” as its theme, exploring the ideas and mastery behind the objects on view. I’m particularly excited to see Alma Berrow ’s playful ceramics at Megan Mulrooney ’s debut Design Miami presentation, staged as a table set for a feast. The fair is also a hotbed of brand collaborations, including a Kohler installation that delves into the company’s archives to trace a century of color in its designs. The fair opens with an invitation-only preview on December 1st, followed by public admission December 2nd–6th. 5. Marcel Dzama, “Who Loves the Moon?” Dec. 3–4 | 434 Lincoln Rd. | Miami Beach The fantastical world of Marcel Dzama comes to life in “Who Loves the Moon?,” an ambitious installation presented by Capital One and The Cultivist. Known for his whimsical, surreal characters that inhabit a theatrical dream world, Dzama pushes his work into new dimensions through intricate environments and performances. Visitors enter through the mouth of a giant moon before exploring interconnected rooms, featuring puppetry and a grand chess hall. The project also includes performances by Miami City Ballet, with costumes designed by Dzama. The experience is free with advance RSVP. 6. ICA Miami 61 NE 41st St. | Miami Design District The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami is always worth a visit during Miami Art Week, and this year’s winter exhibitions are especially promising. A highlight is Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë ’s first solo museum exhibition in the U.S., organized with the Fondation Cartier. The show brings together more than 100 works by the Venezuelan Yanomami artist, whose practice reflects the natural world and his community’s cultural traditions. The museum also hosts a new commission by Naudline Pierre , whose paintings fill the museum’s three-story stairwell, while Carroll Dunham presents his first painting survey at a museum in more than 25 years. Other exhibitions spotlight Diego Singh and Ernie Barnes ’s iconic painting The Sugar Shack (1976). Nearby, in the museum’s Expansion Building, Friedrich Kunath presents “I’ll Romanticize This Later,” a career-spanning survey of paintings, sculptures, and installations. 7. Rubell Museum 1100 NW 23rd St. | Allapattah I always try to make time for the Rubell Museum, home to one of the country’s most significant private collections of contemporary art. On December 1st, the museum unveils a new slate of exhibitions, including presentations by its recent artists-in-residence. I’m especially keen to see rising painter Reginald Sylvester II ’s “Wise Men Mad.” Also on view are presentations featuring Hernan Bas , Robert Colescott , Barkley L. Hendricks , and Mickalene Thomas , alongside recent acquisitions and the museum’s ever-popular Yayoi Kusama works, including her mirrored silver orbs and two Infinity Rooms. If you have time while you’re in Allapattah, head to nearby galleries like Mindy Solomon Gallery and Andrew Reed Gallery , and private collection spaces including El Espacio 23 and Márquez Art Projects. 8. The Bass 2100 Collins Ave. | Miami Beach Between fairs on Miami Beach, head to The Bass for an intriguing lineup of shows. Japanese artist Yuko Mohri turns everyday objects into playful, kinetic sculptures, while Amalia Pica ’s “Lecturas Posibles” fills the museum’s new Rotunda gallery with a library of chalkboards where visitors can add their own drawings and writing. Also worth seeing are Sarah Zapata ’s monumental textiles, which draw on her Peruvian heritage, and Pedro y Juana’s “Aquí,” an immersive installation inspired by Miami Beach and Mexico City. 9. Creative Time Sandcastle Competition Dec. 1, 2:30–4:30 p.m. | The Miami Beach EDITION, 2901 Collins Ave. | Miami Beach For something a little different, head to the beach for Creative Time’s Sandcastle Competition, making its Miami debut after years at Rockaway Beach in New York. Participating artists include Emmett Moore , Jillian Mayer , Theresa Chromati , and Gabriel Rico , who will create ephemeral sculptures in the sand. Judges include designer Rafael de Cárdenas , artist Michi Jigarjian, and curator Kimberly Drew. 10. Faena Art Dec. 1–6, 12–9 p.m. | Faena Beach and Faena Cathedral, Collins Ave. | Miami Beach Just up Collins Avenue from the sandcastle competition, Faena Art presents two ambitious public art installations, both free to visit. On the beach, Christopher Joshua Benton ’s A Lore Supreme (2026), his first major U.S. installation, takes the form of a monumental mirrored sphere, 44 feet wide, emerging from the sand. Its 7,000 reflective facets shimmer in the wind like a giant disco ball that doubles as a stage for performances, including DJ sets by Major Lazer, Richie Hell, and DJ Le Spam. Inside the Faena Cathedral, Marinella Senatore ’s An Expanded Baroque Crown (2026) draws inspiration from the festivals and street celebrations of southern Italy. The illuminated installation also serves as a venue for readings and performances.

title: Nick Cave and Indian pavilion awarded Venice Biennale 2026’s “Visitor Lions” prizes.
summary: American artist Nick Cave and the Indian pavilion have been awarded the Visitors’ Lions at the 2026 Venice Biennale . La Biennale di Venezia announced the winners on November 25th, three days after the 61st edition of the international art exhibition closed to the public. Cave received the award for best participant in “ In Minor Keys ,” the central exhibition conceived by the late curator Koyo Kouoh , while India received the award for best national participation. The prizes were determined by votes cast by ticket holders who visited both the Giardini and Arsenale between May 9th and November 22nd. The Visitors’ Lions were introduced this year following the resignation of the Biennale’s international jury in April. The awards replaced the traditional jury-selected Golden and Silver Lions amid controversy surrounding the participation of Russia and Israel. At the Arsenale, Cave presented Two Points in Time—At Once (2026), a series of monumental bronze sculptures and mixed-media installations that allude to the seven stages of grief. The Chicago-based artist, best known for his elaborate wearable sculptures called “ Soundsuits ,” incorporated floral motifs, needlepoint self-portraits, and found domestic objects into the presentation, exploring the relationship between mourning and remembrance. India’s Biennale exhibition, “Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home,” marked the country’s return to the event after a seven-year absence. Curated by Amin Jaffer, the pavilion brought together five artists: Alwar Balasubramaniam , Sumakshi Singh , Ranjani Shettar , Asim Waqif , and Skarma Sonam Tashi. It was named one of Artsy’s 10 best national pavilions at this year’s Biennale. Exploring notions of home and belonging through materials rooted in Indian craft traditions, the exhibition featured Singh’s embroidered reconstruction of her demolished family home in New Delhi and Waqif’s expansive bamboo installation, assembled on-site at the Arsenale. “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition—the Visitors’ Award—as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso ’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it,” said La Biennale di Venezia president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco in a statement. “I can say without hesitation that La Biennale is brimming with ever-renewed energy thanks to the vibrant presence of everyone.”

title: Thelma Golden will step down as director of the Studio Museum in Harlem in 2027.
summary: Thelma Golden will step down as director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem in late 2027, the museum has announced. Board chair Kathryn C. Chenault said trustees had accepted Golden's plan, which she shared a year after her 20th anniversary in the job and the opening of the museum’s new building on West 125th Street in 2025. Founded in 1968, the Studio Museum is in its 58th year and will mark its 60th anniversary under new leadership. The board, which numbers 31 voting trustees, has set up a search committee and brought in an international search firm to help find her replacement. Golden will stay on until a new director is in place and will help with the handover. The museum has not named candidates or a target date for the hire. “I know this is the right moment to begin this transition,” Golden said in a statement. She thanked the mentors, trustees, staff, Harlem neighbors, and artists who shaped the institution, and said that community would sustain whoever leads it next. Chenault said Golden had shaped the museum’s vision and identity for more than two decades, pushed Black artists toward the center of the culture, and mentored a generation of Black museum professionals nationwide. Golden, Chenault said, is now handing the museum to the people she helped bring up. Golden’s ties to the museum go back to her undergraduate years at Smith College in Massachusetts, when she interned there; she stayed on as a curatorial fellow after she graduated. She moved to the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988, where she co-organized the 1993 Whitney Biennial with Elisabeth Sussman and staged the 1994 show “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art.” She came back to the Studio Museum in 2000 as deputy director for exhibitions and programs, and took over as director when Lowery Stokes Sims left in 2005. A decade into the job, she looked back with Artsy on her tenure and on the changing face of Harlem. Her 2001 exhibition “Freestyle,” co-curated with Christine Y. Kim, launched the museum's "F" shows of emerging Black artists, each named after a concept beginning with the letter. While the museum was closed for construction, Golden kept it visible through inHarlem, a series of projects with neighborhood partners, and a multiyear partnership with MoMA and MoMA PS1 . There she organized shows of Michael Armitage , Ming Smith , and Tadáskía . In 2023, she became the first arts administrator to win the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize . The new building, the first the museum has built for its own use, opened on November 15, 2025. The Creating Space campaign behind it has raised $322 million to date, and the endowment has grown to $95 million, up from $5 million when the board approved the building project. The collection also grew under Golden, through purchases, gifts from artists, and the Peggy Cooper Cafritz bequest .

title: Frieze Los Angeles announces 102 galleries for 2027 edition.
summary: Frieze Los Angeles has announced 102 galleries for its 2027 edition. The exhibiting galleries will represent 20 countries, including 38 galleries with spaces in Los Angeles, and will include 22 first-time exhibitors. The fair will take place at Santa Monica Airport from February 25th to 28th. This year, Focus—the fair's section for solo presentations by US-based galleries founded within the past 12 years—will be curated by Erin Christovale of the Hammer Museum . Focused on emerging galleries, 10 of the 15 galleries participating in Focus are new to the fair, including Rajiv Menon Contemporary and Megan Mulrooney . International blue-chip galleries will be strongly represented, with Gagosian , Hauser & Wirth , Lisson , Pace Gallery , Sprüth Magers , White Cube , and David Zwirner among those participating. Los Angeles mainstays such as Château Shatto, Anat Ebgi , François Ghebaly, Regen Projects, and Luis De Jesus Los Angeles will also be in attendance. Meanwhile, at the fair’s entrance, Los Angeles artist rafa esparza will unveil Queercancha , a new work painted across two adobe panels mounted on chrome steel armatures. The work is based on a photograph of queer friends driving through Los Angeles in a convertible. A related painting, WeDGAF (2026), will appear on billboards and digital screens across the city during Frieze Week through a partnership with Orange Barrel Media. Esparza is represented by Commonwealth and Council and recently joined Hauser & Wirth. Deutsche Bank, marking its 24th year as Frieze's global lead partner, will present its 2027 Artist of the Year, Tania Franco Klein , in its lounge for the first time. Deutsche Bank Frieze Los Angeles Film Award, in collaboration with Ghetto Film School, will also return with a short-film fellowship and competition for emerging Los Angeles filmmakers. This December, in advance of the fair, Frieze Los Angeles will also announce the recipient of its Impact Prize, presented with NXTHVN and supported by WME Impact. The winner will receive $25,000, a solo presentation, and curatorial mentorship. As part of the greater Los Angeles Art Week, Frieze Los Angeles will coincide with other fairs taking place across the city, including Felix Art Fair , Post-Fair, the Other Art Fair, and Enzo.

title: 8 Rising Latin American Indigenous Artists to Know
summary: As a group, Latin American Indigenous artists may be more different than they are the same. After all, they could come from any one of 20 countries, each of which is home to scores of individual Indigenous cultures, all with distinct histories, landscapes, economies, and religious practices. But curator Raphael Fonseca—who has spent the last five years traveling the Western Hemisphere and acquiring objects for the Denver Art Museum—is focused on the similarities. Chief among them is the impact that European colonialism, which began five centuries ago, has had, and continues to have, on these artists’ communities. It is a shared experience that goes beyond territorial borders. These artists have another thing in common, according to Fonseca: After being long overlooked by the global art world, their work is now in demand as collectors and museums look to diversify and balance their holdings. That has given them, to some degree, a collective identity. “As an organized movement of people saying ‘I’m Indigenous and I’m also a contemporary artist’—that is something that has only been happening for real in the last 10 years,” he said. Fonseca, who is Brazilian, was appointed the Denver museum’s first-ever curator of modern and contemporary Latin American art in 2021 and given the mandate of honing its collection. He began an extensive buying mission, the results of which have culminated in the exhibit “I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America,” which continues through July 11, 2027. The show features more than 100 works from 50 artists, most from the museum’s own collection, and includes many rising names. Some artists are just emerging, others have been working for decades but only recently received wider recognition. Here are eight Latin American Indigenous artists who stand out right now. Elyla B. 1989, Chontales, Nicaragua. Lives and works between Masaya, Nicaragua, and Basel. Through dramatic videos and performance pieces, Elyla has emerged as a crucial figure in bringing international attention to contemporary artists in Nicaragua. Born in Chontales, the home region of the Chontal people, the artist re-imagines long-standing colonial narratives and native rituals in beautiful-yet-dark cinematic works that explore what it means to be mestiza (mixed European and Indigenous). The 2024 video Tierra Retumbante (Rumbling Earth) , for example, was filmed on the top of Nicaragua’s active Masaya Volcano, and features sweeping, aerial views of Elyla singing and whistling, wearing traditional sandals that have been converted into leather high heels. Elyla’s pieces have appeared at recent biennials in Havana, Guatemala City, and Toronto. Meanwhile, the Museum of Modern Art in New York just snapped up their work Torita Encuetada (2023), shown at the Venice Biennale 2024 , which puts a contemporary spin on an ancient fire ritual. Tall, beaded and often wearing all-black, Elyla has a commanding personal presence that comes alive on-stage and on-camera. Julia Isídrez B. 1967, Ita, Paraguay. Lives and works in Ita. Cantaro con relieve, 2024 Julia Isídrez Olney Gleason Also included in the Venice Biennale 2024, Julia Isídrez carries on a long tradition of ceramic making, often handed down mother-to-daughter, that is practiced by the Guaraní people in Paraguay. Isídrez learned this skill from her own mother, Juana Marta Rodas, and the pair worked collaboratively until Rodas’s death in 2013, making objects that rely on ancient techniques, familiar forms, and local materials. Rather than employing these techniques for their usual purposes—as bowls, cooking vessels, or other functional items—Isídrez makes art works. Her piece in “I Follow Rivers,” titled El mundo de Julia (Julia’s World) (2024) is a good example. The object takes the shape of a common vase, though there is no opening for flowers. Instead, Isídrez crowns the piece with the heads of tiny creatures. Like many of her creations, it references personal and regional history while pushing an age-old art form in contemporary directions. “She is very famous, though she has only had market recognition for maybe two years now,” said Fonseca. “Three years ago, you could buy a piece of hers in Paraguay for $100. Now they are $15,000.” Rosa Elena Curruchich B. 1958, Comalapa, Guatemala. D. 2005, Comalapa. Rosa Elena Curruchich was a Maya Kaqchikel artist who lived in Guatemala from 1958 to 2005, and who has only recently been discovered by curators and collectors. Her heavily detailed oil-on-canvas paintings document the lives of women in her community. In some, they perform everyday chores like washing clothes in a river, in others, they celebrate weddings and religious ceremonies. Discouraged from painting because of her gender and social class, she worked in secret and created only small pieces—many 8-by-8 inches or less—so she could more easily conceal and transport them. Curruchich’s work was researched and championed by the Guatemala City gallery Proyectos Ultravioleta which began showing her at art fairs in 2024. Since then her paintings have been acquired by Tate Modern and the Centre Pompidou. She was included in the main exhibit at the 2024 Venice Biennale and recently had solo shows at Museo Universitario del Chopo, Mexico City, and the Museu de Arte de São Paulo. Seba Calfuqueo B. 1991, Santiago, Chile. Lives and works in Santiago. Mapuche artist Seba Calfuqueo is best known for lush, romantic, sensual and richly colored videos, set in jungles and rivers in Chile’s La Araucanía Region and other tropical locations. But Calfuqueo also works in ceramics, performance, photography and 3-D animation, often re-interpreting Mapuche cosmology with a goal of confronting the exploitation of people and lands during the colonial era and challenging gender-binary stereotypes. Her animated 2022 video in the Denver exhibition is a good example. Titled Ngüru Ka Willin, (Fox and Otter) , the four-minute piece gives a contemporary queer spin to a century-old Chilean folktale. Her videos were included in the most recent Whitney Biennial and featured in presentations at Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles and Madrid’s Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza. Santiago Yahuarcani B. 1960, Pucaurquillo, Peru. Lives and works in Pucaurquillo. At 66, Santiago Yahuarcani has been exhibiting in his native country of Peru for decades, where the artist and activist is seen as an “icon,” according to Fonseca. Yahuarcani is known for his detailed mystical paintings that mingle old traditions with present-day social and political ideas. For example, he uses natural inks to paint on organic canvases made of bark (called Ilanchama ) and his works reference Aimeni cosmology (the clan to which he belongs). His career has taken off in the last five years with a number of solo shows in Latin America and Europe, and acquisitions by Tate Modern, MoMA, Museo Reina Sofía, and other notable institutions. Claudia Alarcón B. 1989, La Puntana, Argentina. Lives and works in Santa Victoria Este, Argentina. A textile artist from the La Puntana community of Wichí people based in northern Argentina, Claudia Alarcón is known for both solo work and her collaborations. In particular, she has often worked with Silät, a regional collective of 100-plus women, founded in 2023, who practice traditional weaving relying primarily on chaguar fibers. Chaguar, extracted from local bromeliad plants, was used for generations in the making of functional objects like bags and blankets, but Alarcón alters traditional threads and patterns to create colorful, abstract, politically-conscious tapestries that have found their way into collections of the Guggenheim , LACMA , and the Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires. Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë B. 1971, Sheroana, Venezuela. Lives and works in Mahekoto-Theri, Venezuela. A Yanomami painter and papermaker in the Venezuelan Amazon, Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë creates a minimalist effect in his works, relying on bold colors and simple shapes to depict regional plants, animals, and humans in an abstract way. “I Follow Rivers” presents a series of drawings from 2019, all made with oil-based ink applied to paper fabricated from mulberry bark. The grid-like drawings unfurl in rhythmic shapes and patterns that appear as codes—but whose titles give them away as Hakihiiwë’s versions of butterflies, toucans and caterpillars. The works play with “different traditions of Indigenous art in Venezuela, but I think he plays in a very free way,” said Fonseca. “And everything is handcrafted.” The Pérez Art Museum in Miami and Peru’s Museo de Arte de Lima are among the institutions that have collected his work. Pamela Cevallos B. 1984, Quito, Ecuador. Lives and works in Quito. Pamela Cevallos is an Ecuadorian artist and researcher who has worked closely with artisans from La Pila, a community within the Manabí province, who maintain strong connections to Indigenous Manteño traditions. Artists there are known for creating ceramic replicas of lost (or pillaged) artifacts, a practice that Cevallos also draws on. Her ceramic pieces in this exhibition—doll-like figures with colorful painted faces standing just over 2 feet tall—continue the practice of recreating artifacts. In this way, the artist questions authenticity, ownership and curatorial authority. In addition to her art, she helped to establish the Historical and Artisanal Museum of La Pila, which displays locally-made replicas to the public.

title: What Sold at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026
summary: Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 closed on Sunday, November 22nd, with galleries reporting several sellout presentations and sales to private and institutional collections. The inaugural edition of the fair, which took over from Abu Dhabi Art , featured 89 exhibitors. Visitors from more than 75 countries attended the fair’s venue, Manarat Al Saadiyat, over its four-day run, according to organizers. Among the institutions represented at the fair were Louvre Abu Dhabi, the British Museum , the Guggenheim Museum , the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , and Qatar Museums’ Art Mill Museum. Sales reported by galleries pointed to a strong market among collectors in the region. Victoria Miro , for instance, reported a near-sellout of its booth with the majority of works placed in collections in the U.A.E. “Frieze Abu Dhabi was an all-round excellent experience for us and the most transactional fair we have done in the region,” said Glenn Scott Wright, president of Victoria Miro. The inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi was considerably smaller than its predecessor, which featured 142 galleries last year. The fair’s more tightly curated format emphasized artists from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia, and sales across the week suggested that this approach resonated with collectors. “It has been wonderful to see the response from the local community and their engagement with the artists we are showing. The collector base here is educated, eager to learn, and enthusiastic, which is not always the case with other fairs we do,” said Niamh Coghlan, senior director at Richard Saltoun . Some of the fair’s most compelling presentations were those that engaged directly with the region’s cultural histories. That theme also extended to the fair’s Frieze Masters section, curated by Marika Sardar, which explores the artistic exchange around the Indian Ocean. Among the most significant reported transactions at the fair was David Aaron’s seven-figure sale of a 2,000-year-old monument from ancient Yemen, which had returned to the Arabian Peninsula for the first time in nearly 70 years. Here is a breakdown of the sales reported by galleries at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026. Leading sales at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 Thaddaeus Ropac sold three sculptures from Imran Qureshi ’s “Water Bodies” series for $60,000 apiece to U.A.E.-based collections. P420 sold nine works at the fair, including Irma Blank ’s Radical Writings, Abecedarium 12-02-91 (1991) for $170,000. Kó reported sales of “several” works by two artists: Wooden wall works by Ato Ribeiro totaling $75,000. Works by Ben Osawe totaling $125,000. Sold-out booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 La Cañada, 2026 Hilary Pecis Timothy Taylor Guest Room Chair, 2026 Hilary Pecis Timothy Taylor Several galleries reported sold-out presentations at the inaugural edition of the fair, with solo booths proving particularly successful. Taymour Grahne Projects , one of Artsy’s five best booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 , sold out its solo presentation of mosaic works by Ala Younis depicting Abu Dhabi’s modernist architecture. Timothy Taylor sold out its solo presentation of works by Hilary Pecis , including one work acquired by a regional institution. Other works were placed in collections across the U.A.E., Asia, the U.S., and the U.K. Johyun Gallery sold out its solo presentation of works by Lee Bae for undisclosed prices. Abu Dhabi–based gallery Iris Projects sold out its booth for undisclosed prices. Several other galleries reported near-sellout booths: Victoria Miro “nearly” sold out its booth featuring works by N.S. Harsha , Idris Khan , and Yayoi Kusama . Tabari sold the “majority” of its booth on the opening day of the fair, including works by Irene Scheinmann , Hazem Harb , and Khaled Zaki . More sales reported at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 Gagosian sold many works from its solo presentation of Roy Lichtenstein for undisclosed prices. Perrotin reported sales of works by Iván Argote , Holly Lowen , and Nancy Graves . Prices were not disclosed. Richard Saltoun Gallery sold works by all six artists featured in its booth: Reena Saini Kallat , Juliana Seraphim , Fathi Hassan , Basil Alkazzi , Marta Roberti , and Everlyn Nicodemus . Prices were undisclosed. Lawrie Shabibi sold all of the works by Hamra Abbas featured in its booth, alongside two steel sculptures by Shaikha Al Mazrou . Prices were not shared. Aisha Alabbar Gallery sold five works from its solo presentation of Abdullah Al Saadi . The Third Line sold a sculpture by Kamran Samimi , featured in Frieze Sculpture Abu Dhabi, to U.A.E. property developer Aldar. Prices were not disclosed. In the fair’s Global Futures section, Zawyeh Gallery sold 12 works by Mohammed Joha . Also in Global Futures, Artwin Gallery sold 10 works from its solo presentation of Almagul Menlibayeva , seven of which were acquired by a private museum in Georgia. Prices were not disclosed. In the Focus section dedicated to emerging galleries, W–Galería sold a textile work by Chosun Bensho to the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. Another work was placed in an Emirati collection. Prices were not disclosed.

title: Art Basel Hong Kong announces 232 galleries for 2027 edition.
summary: Art Basel Hong Kong has announced 232 exhibitors for its 2027 edition. The galleries represent more than 40 countries and territories, and will include 31 first-time exhibitors. The fair will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre from March 25th to 27th with invitation-only preview days on March 23rd and 24th. For 2027, the fair is introducing a refreshed show floor layout intended to create a more focused and intuitive visitor experience. The fair’s special sectors—Discoveries, Insights, Zero 10, and Echoes—will all be presented on Level 3 of the convention center. “The most important and innovative dialogues emerge at the intersection of different worlds, where artistic, cultural, and business communities come together to generate new ideas, perspectives, and opportunities for exchange,” said Angelle Siyang-Le, director of Art Basel Hong Kong, who added that the redesigned floor plan is intended to foster discovery and engagement. More than half of participating galleries operate spaces in the Asia Pacific region. Some 27 galleries at the fair operate spaces in Hong Kong—among them Alisan Fine Arts , Blindspot Gallery , and Empty Gallery . Some 32 galleries are from mainland China; 20 are from Japan, including Taka Ishii Gallery ; 16 are from South Korea, including Kukje Gallery and PKM Gallery ; and eight are from Taiwan. Notable first-time exhibitors include Galerie Nordenhake , Yares Art , Richard Saltoun Gallery , and VeneKlasen . Returning for its second edition, Zero 10, which is focused on digital art, will be curated by Sunny Cheung, independent curator and former curator of design and architecture at M+ , Hong Kong. Discoveries, presenting solo booths of emerging artists, will feature a significant number of first-time exhibitors, with more than half of participating galleries making their debut at the fair. Encounters, dedicated to large-scale installations, sculptures, and performances, will once again be led by Mami Kataoka, director of Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum , alongside Isabella Tam, Alia Swastika, and Hirokazu Tokuyama. Pioneering media artist Ellen Pau will return as curator for the Film program. Insights, focused on cutting-edge art across Asia and the Asia Pacific region, will feature 18 presentations spanning Sri Lanka, Greater China, South Korea, and Japan.

title: Jem Perucchini’s Jewel-Like Portraits Give Black Figures a Place in the Renaissance
summary: Sospiro, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner The Italian Renaissance, Ethiopian Orthodox painting, and African textiles: This is the wide range of inspirations that Italian Ethiopian artist Jem Perucchini draws on in his dazzling portraits. In these works, Perucchini depicts Black figures who, historically, have been marginalized or altogether excluded from the Western European canon. Rendered in jewel-like colors and intricate, dappled textures, his enigmatic scenes inhabit a space between past and present, breathing new life into familiar art historical traditions. Trained at Milan’s Accademia di Belle Arti di Brera, his engagement with art history began long before his formal education. As he recalled in an interview, his earliest encounters with art came through the books, catalogues, and encyclopedias he discovered at his maternal grandfather’s house. These became a kind of visual archive, opening up a world of images, artists, and historical periods, shaping his imagination and relationship with painting. This early curiosity continues to inform his practice today, which is now receiving new attention. Following exhibitions at Corvi-Mora gallery, he was commissioned by Art on the Underground to create Rebirth of a Nation , a major public artwork at Brixton Underground station in 2023. This month, he opened “ Sospiro ,” on view through December 19th, his debut exhibition with David Zwirner in New York, his first exhibition in the United States. Echo and Narcissus, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner The Loss, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner For Perucchini, reimagining the canon of Western art history is not about rejecting tradition, but finding ways to keep its dialogue alive. “I find it more interesting to recover themes, images, and situations that have shaped this culture and make them relevant again by bringing them into dialogue with contemporary sensibilities,” he explained. “Tradition should not be something to preserve unchanged, but rather a language that is still capable of generating new meanings.” With this in mind, I asked the artist which historical works he continues to return to. “ Fra Angelico ’s Annunciation and Piero della Francesca ’s Baptism of Christ and Nativity . These works possess an almost timeless quality, in which formal construction and spiritual depth coexist with remarkable naturalness,” he said. These references are particularly visible in Echo and Narcissus (2026) where the lofty mythological figures are humanized in unceremonious poses. This timelessness is everywhere in “Sospiro.” Here, the works resist an explicit narrative. In fact, Perucchini would prefer for time not to be present at all. “I am interested in creating a condition of temporal suspension, in which the figures seem removed from the flow of events and from any reference to a before or an after,” he said. Rather than inviting the viewer to reconstruct an action or follow a story, he wants the image to be encountered in a kind of “absolute present.” “It is a dimension in which time seems to stand still, leaving room for contemplation.” The Whistler, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner Premonition (Icarus), 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner That idea is also communicated in the exhibition’s title, “Sospiro,” the Italian word for “sigh.” “A sigh is an expression of life through breath,” he explained. “It is a breath that leaves the body and makes perceptible, for a brief moment, something that normally remains invisible: our inner life. The sigh thus becomes a minimal gesture, yet one charged with meaning, capable of making something profoundly intimate visible.” This sense of intimacy is reinforced by the composition of his portraits. “A closer perspective can generate a sense of intimacy and concentration,” he said. “I am interested in making the framing more than just a compositional choice, allowing it to also shape the narrative and emotional perception of the painting.” Color also contributes significantly to the works’ emotional resonance. Compared with earlier works, Perucchini used a broader range of hues for this exhibition, moving between bright, saturated colors and darker, deeper tones. Across the exhibition, moments of luminous intensity alternate with more intimate, nocturnal scenes, creating subtle emotional shifts. The paintings also have a striking jewel-like surface, achieved through the layering of numerous highly diluted applications of color, using a technique known as glazing. Each layer gradually transforms the perception of the one beneath it, producing depth, transparency, and subtle variations in luminosity. “I am especially interested in the way light passes through these layers of color, creating an almost material and precious quality that can recall certain stones or mineral surfaces,” Perucchini said. Equally important is the treatment of pattern and textiles, where the artist takes care to ensure that patterns are rarely repeated. His references range from the graphic motifs of African wax fabrics to the geometric patterns of the Ethiopian Habesha kemis , alongside the two-dimensional decorative language of garments depicted in 14th-century Sienese painting. Spherical, orb-like objects recur again and again. For example, in A Nocturnal Journey (2025), an incandescent, cocoa-colored orb sits neatly on top of an intarsia panel, echoed by the glowing moon above. Ever the polymath, Perucchini tells me that their significance is connected to the Greek philosopher Parmenides, for whom the sphere represented unity. “I am interested in this opposition between a perfect, complete form and everything that surrounds it,” Perucchini explained, “because it makes visible the distance between that which exists in a state of completeness and that which, instead, appears unfinished.”

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Miami
summary: Year-round sunshine, miles of coastline, a culture steeped in Latin American influence, a world-class restaurant scene, and neighborhoods anchored by galleries, museums, and public art draw travelers to Miami. For art lovers, few U.S. cities offer as much. Since 2002, Art Basel Miami Beach—the Americas’ leading art fair—and satellites like Untitled Art, NADA, and Design Miami, all held the first week of December, have made the city the art world's favorite winter escape. But a week isn't nearly enough to see everything. "Miami has developed a robust, year-round arts calendar, so there's really no bad time to visit," said local gallerist Anthony Spinello . No matter the season, you'll encounter ambitious institutional shows, bold private collections, and a dynamic community of artists working in studios across Miami—many of whom welcome visitors. Here’s what art lovers need to know. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Miami Miami’s art scene stretches across the city, but four areas stand out: Miami Beach, with its oceanfront art and Art Deco architecture; fast-growing Allapattah; the polished Design District; and neighboring Little Haiti and Little River, where many galleries and nonprofits have settled. Miami Beach Most know Miami Beach as the home of Art Basel, but the area’s art scene reaches well beyond the convention center. In Mid-Beach, Faena Art stages ambitious installations and performances across the Faena hotel and district. Farther south, The Bass presents contemporary art in a 1930s Art Deco building. Chloe Berkowitz, a collector and president of the Berkowitz Contemporary Foundation, recommends a route that links the two, starting at Faena and following the beachwalk south to The Bass. “It’s a beautiful way to take in the ocean and the architecture of Miami Beach while discovering art along the way,” she said. A few blocks inland on Lincoln Road, Oolite Arts is a beloved nonprofit that has given resident artists free studio space and exhibited their work for more than four decades. Allapattah The Rubell Museum fills a former industrial complex in the steadily rising neighborhood. Nearby, El Espacio 23 , the contemporary art space founded by collector Jorge Pérez, hosts artists in residence alongside its exhibitions. Local artist Joyce Billiet recommends starting at the Rubell and wandering on foot to “discover some of the galleries scattered throughout the neighborhood.” Set among warehouses, produce markets, and the Latino bakeries that give Allapattah its character are tastemaking commercial galleries like Mindy Solomon , Spinello Projects , Andrew Reed , KDR , and Voloshyn . Miami Design District Anchored by ICA Miami , a free-admission museum, the Design District is known above all for its "robust collection of public artworks permanently on view," said Karen Grimson, the district's director of art and culture. "Walk around, and you'll find everything from benches designed by Zaha Hadid to a mural by John Baldessari or a sculpture by Urs Fischer ," adds Billiet, who recommends signing up for the neighborhood's public art walking tours. Little Haiti and Little River Just north of the Design District, these two adjoining neighborhoods—once largely industrial—have drawn many of the city's most respected galleries and nonprofits into their converted warehouses. In Little Haiti, Nina Johnson ’s sprawling four-building compound includes a backyard house turned gallery, redesigned by the architecture studio Charlap Hyman & Herrero. Little River is home to Dot Fiftyone and Primary , alongside nonprofit art spaces like Locust Projects and Dimensions Variable . The museums and galleries to know in Miami Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Miami’s flagship art museum is housed in a Herzog & de Meuron building where hanging gardens sway above shaded verandas and slender columns frame sweeping views of Biscayne Bay. The PAMM collection places particular emphasis on artists from Latin America and the Caribbean. ICA Miami. Known for giving rising names like Miami’s own Rose Marie Cromwell their first museum shows, while also mounting surveys of established figures such as Betye Saar and Olga de Amaral . Its next chapter arrives in late 2027, when a Gensler-designed expansion next door will double its space and put its collection on permanent view for the first time. The Bass. Miami Beach’s contemporary art museum runs an ongoing “Miami Years” series, which devotes an annual solo show to a single artist's ties to the city. Past editions have featured Nam June Paik and Rachel Feinstein . Nearby in Collins Park, the Rotunda—the old public library's 1962 assembly room—now serves as the museum's satellite gallery. Spinello Projects . Founded in 2005 and now based in Allapattah, Spinello Projects is part gallery, part nomadic platform for site-specific and curatorial projects that often take place beyond its own walls. Many of its artists are Miami-based, including Elliot & Erick Jiménez , Marlon Portales , and Nina Surel . David Castillo. The first Miami gallery to show at Art Basel in Switzerland, David Castillo has a reputation for spotting talent early—many major artists began their careers with the gallery. Its roster includes Sanford Biggers and Lyle Ashton Harris , as well as the estate of Cuban printmaker Belkis Ayón . Nina Johnson. Miami native Nina Johnson opened her gallery in Wynwood in 2007 and has since built it into one of the city’s most respected. Now based in Little Haiti, it shows contemporary names like Dara Friedman , Katie Stout , and Emmett Moore alongside trailblazing figures like Judy Chicago . Mindy Solomon. A regular at Design Miami, Mindy Solomon brought her gallery from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Allapattah, where it shows artists from emerging to well-established with a strong eye for ceramics and craft. Its program includes Linda Lopez , Lisu Vega , and Amber Cowan . Bakehouse Art Complex.
