Artists took over this 1926 Art Deco bakery in 1985, long before Wynwood became an art destination, and it remains one of the city’s most important nonprofit studio complexes. Some 60 studios sit alongside two galleries, so visitors can move straight from an exhibition to the studios where the work is being made. And beyond. Institutions that reward a detour include the MOCA North Miami , Vizcaya Museum and Gardens , and the University of Miami’s Lowe Art Museum , which Berkowitz calls “an unexpected gem.” Smaller specialist collections include The Wolfsonian–FIU , devoted to design and decorative arts, The Margulies Collection at the WAREhOUSE , and the Frost Art Museum at Florida International University . For something off the usual circuit, Grimson recommends Collective 62 , a space run by women artists in Liberty City. Where the art world in Miami eats, drinks, and shops The art world’s dining picks in Miami span Michelin-starred kitchens, oceanfront institutions, and neighborhood counters. For dinner In Little River, Sunny’s draws a steady stream of artists and collectors for steaks and a famously good playlist. "It's certainly not a secret anymore, and getting a table can be an adventure, but I have to say, it really does live up to the hype," said Berkowitz. Close by, Michelin-starred Boia De serves inventive Italian cooking from a tiny space tucked into a Buena Vista strip mall. In the Design District, Spinello's go-to is Mother Wolf , a Roman restaurant as notable for its interiors as for its pasta. For a special occasion, The Surf Club Restaurant —Thomas Keller's elegant ode to mid-century glamour inside the Four Seasons in Surfside—sets the scene for a long, celebratory dinner. Back in Miami Beach, local favorite Macchialina serves handmade pastas with a neighborhood feel. For lunch At the other end of the spectrum, Berkowitz heads to Enriqueta’s Sandwich Shop for medianoches and croquetas. “You'll find people from every walk of life sitting alongside one another, enjoying a meal that's so deeply connected to Miami's identity,” she said. For drinks Miami’s cocktail scene has anchors worth knowing. Broken Shaker at Freehand Miami remains the destination for industry-caliber drinks, while Sweet Liberty on Miami Beach has anchored the local scene for over a decade. For a hotel bar with art world crossover, the Living Room at Faena Hotel is ideal— Damien Hirst ’s gold mammoth presides over the pool, and the Juan Gatti -painted ceilings are worth a visit in their own right. For browsing Miami has a small but devoted independent book scene. In the Design District, Dale Zine —a favorite of both Billiet and Grimson—stocks art books, exhibition catalogs, and zines from small presses alongside work by Miami artists. In Little Haiti, EXILE Books , founded by artist Amanda Keeley after years at New York’s Printed Matter, specializes in artists' books and publishes them under its own imprint. For a broader selection, Books & Books , a local institution since 1982, is worth the drive to its flagship on Aragon Avenue in Coral Gables. On Biscayne Boulevard, Fly Boutique has been a fixture of the MiMo District for years. Spinello calls it “a treasure trove of expertly curated vintage designer clothing, accessories, and unique furniture.” Little River is becoming a shopping destination in its own right: Homegrown label Eliou , known for handcrafted jewelry and contemporary fashion with a following well beyond Miami, has kept a storefront in the neighborhood for several years. Down the street, Reserved brings vintage clothing, vinyl, and hi-fi listening together under one roof, while Casa de Barcelona specializes in restored mid-century and postmodern furniture. Where to stay Faena Hotel Miami Beach is the art-forward natural fit, with Faena Art active across the hotel and district. For a design-led alternative, 1 Hotel South Beach leans eco-forward. For art world proximity, the Albion Hotel sits beside the Rubell Museum in Allapattah. Top tips for art lovers visiting Miami When to go Art Week is the high point of Miami’s art calendar, but for a less frenetic visit, Billiet and Spinello both suggest early fall, when the new exhibition season gets underway after the summer lull. Grimson makes the case for January and February, when the weather is ideal for walking and many of the season's strongest shows are still on view. How to navigate Miami is spread out, and traffic can be unpredictable, especially during Art Week. Plan each day around one neighborhood rather than crossing the city repeatedly. Berkowitz recommends the free Miami Beach Water Taxi , which links Sunset Harbour and Edgewater, as a scenic way to skip traffic on the causeways. What locals know In Miami, the studio visit is as much a part of the art calendar as the gallery opening. Open houses at Bakehouse Art Complex and Fountainhead —an artist residency and studio program set to open a new campus in 2027—are the easiest way in, though dates vary, so plan ahead. Just as important are the nonprofits that form the backbone of the local scene. Locust Projects and Oolite Arts , two of the city’s longest-running, have spent decades giving Miami artists the space and support to take risks, and a visit to either offers an insider's look at the city's thriving art scene. Bringing work home Miami is one of the easiest American cities for art logistics. Domestic U.S. shipping is routine, and the city's deep ties to Latin American collectors mean galleries here handle cross-border shipping to and from the region more often than almost anywhere else in the US. English and Spanish are both standard in commercial galleries.

title: 20 New Artist Auction Records Set in November 2026
summary: More than $2 billion worth of art has been auctioned off in New York this week during the annual marquee sale season. This was a week shaped by major collections, including those of philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) trustee Agnes Gund, artist Jeff Koons , and Argentine collectors Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, whose holdings of Impressionist and modern art were among the season’s biggest draws. Christie’s 20th-century evening sale brought in $626.6 million with fees (all listed prices include fees), up from $471.7 million at its equivalent sale last November. The auction was led by Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23), which sold for $85.8 million and nearly doubled the artist’s previous auction record. Another star lot, Gustav Klimt ’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), fetched $82.3 million, while Fernando Botero was among six artists to set new records that evening. The strong sale followed a banner Wednesday that saw the highest ever total for the Impressionist and Modern Art Day and Works on Paper sales at the auction house. Sotheby’s, meanwhile, brought in $777.8 million across two back-to-back evening sales on Wednesday, its highest total for a single evening and surpassing the $706 million achieved during comparable sales last November. The first, “Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection,” was a dedicated sale of 12 Impressionist works assembled by the Argentine couple, which realized $412 million. It was led by Vincent van Gogh ’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which fetched $190.4 million, setting a new auction record for the artist and becoming the second-most-expensive work ever sold at Sotheby’s. The subsequent Modern Evening sale brought in $365.8 million, setting records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas . Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction also produced a slew of auction records for artists including Tomma Abts and Jonas Wood . Elsewhere, Phillips’s modern and contemporary evening sale brought in $104.4 million, up 55 percent year over year, led by Amedeo Modigliani ’s Tête (1911), which fetched $44.6 million. Bonhams’ 20th- and 21st-century evening sale totaled $10 million, led by George Condo ’s Big Face (2015) at $3.4 million, while a dedicated sale of five Constantin Brâncuși pivoted to a private sale in agreement with the consignor. Major single-owner collections continue to power these marquee auctions, with exceptional works and strong provenance continuing to attract buyers despite uneven bidding across the wider market. “It’s been a solid auction week with few surprises—tight, carefully curated sales in which financial guarantees on most top lots ensure the predictability of results,” said Fotini Xydas, head of art finance at Citi Wealth. “The market remains rational and healthy—we’ve seen active participation from buyers globally, record prices achieved at all price levels, and collectors buying with diligence and intentionality. ” Here, we spotlight 20 artist records set during the season. All prices include fees. Vincent van Gogh Châtaigniers en fleurs , 1890 Sold for $190.4 million (Estimate: $180 million) Sotheby’s Painted just four days after Van Gogh’s arrival in Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) (1890) captures a sunlit village street lined with flowering chestnut trees. Three women carrying parasols gather beneath the trees, while a large house rises in the background. The painting belongs to the final, extraordinarily prolific months of the artist’s life, following his departure from a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He died in July 1890, just two months after arriving in Auvers. Owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family since 1975, the painting became the subject of a restitution claim shortly before the auction. Descendants of former owners Hedwig and Samuel Fischer alleged that it had been sold under duress during Nazi persecution in the 1930s. An undisclosed agreement between the heirs and the sellers allowed the sale to proceed. At Sotheby’s New York this week, Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, with veteran dealer William Acquavella winning the bidding. The result marked the f ourth-highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction, surpassing van Gogh’s previous record of $117.2 million, set by Verger avec cyprès (1888) from Paul Allen’s collection at Christie’s New York in 2022. Wassily Kandinsky Betonte Ecken , 1922–1923 Sold for $85.8 million (Estimate: $60 million–$80 million) Christie’s Kandinsky’s auction record has almost doubled in a single evening, thanks to the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922–23). The painting was consigned by the Nahmad family, prominent art dealers and collectors known for their extensive Pablo Picasso holdings and galleries in London and New York. The family acquired it for $1 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1986. It had previously sold at the same auction house in 1964 for $61,000. In 1929, it became the first known Kandinsky painting acquired by Hilla Rebay, the German artist and collector who later advised Solomon R. Guggenheim on building his collection of abstract art. Kandinsky painted Betonte Ecken shortly after joining the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany, in 1922, at the invitation of its founder, Walter Gropius. Measuring just over four feet square, the work marks his shift away from gestural abstraction towards sharply defined geometric forms, reflecting the influence of Suprematism and Constructivism. Its title, translated as “Accentuated corners,” refers to the intersecting lines and colorful shapes that draw attention to the painting’s four corners. Betonte Ecken , which was backed by a guarantee, sold for $85.8 million at Christie’s New York, against an $80 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kandinsky’s previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s London in 2023. Sam Francis Towards Disappearance I , 1958 Sold for $17.13 million (Estimate: $15 million–$20 million) Sotheby’s Painted in 1958 at his studio in Arcueil, France, Towards Disappearance I (1958) dates to one of the most celebrated periods of Sam Francis ’s career. Spanning more than 10 feet in length, the monumental canvas is one of just seven works in the artist’s celebrated “Disappearance” series, three of which are held in major institutional collections, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Across an expansive white ground, clusters of Francis’s signature cobalt blue are punctuated by bursts of yellow and vermilion, reflecting the artist’s exploration of color, space, and the expressive possibilities of abstraction. “When I paint, I try to create the feeling of being in it,” Francis remarked in 1956. Having begun painting in 1944, in his early twenties, Francis drew inspiration from Abstract Expressionists , particularly the organic forms and monumental scale of Clyfford Still’ s canvases and restrained compositions of Mark Rothko . Though he never aligned himself with a single artistic movement, these influences were further shaped by his West Coast roots and his move to France. Acquired by collectors Richard C. and Elizabeth Hedreen at Sotheby’s New York in 1999 for $3.41 million—then an artist record— Towards Disappearance I returned to Sotheby’s this week, selling for $17.1 million against a high estimate of $20 million. The result surpassed Francis’s previous record of $13.6 million, set by Composition in Blue and Black (1955) at Christie’s New York in 2022. Yayoi Kusama No. 3P.B. , 1960 Sold for $15.1 million. (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million) Sotheby’s Just three months after Yayoi Kusama ’s death at age 97 , an early painting from her celebrated “ Infinity Nets ” series has set a new auction record for the Japanese artist. No. 3P.B. (1960) was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s 1961 annual exhibition, one of Kusama’s earliest institutional presentations in the United States. Kusama began her “Infinity Nets” series in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to New York. Inspired in part by the rippling sea she observed during her journey across the Pacific, the paintings feature repeated loops of paint extending across large canvases. No. 3P.B. is an early example, its dense crimson brushstrokes creating a network of overlapping forms. The repetition that defines the series would remain central to Kusama’s practice for more than six decades. No. 3P.B. sold for $15.1 million at Sotheby’s New York, against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kusama’s previous auction record of $10.5 million, set by another early “Infinity Net” painting, Untitled (Nets) (1959), at Phillips New York in 2022. Aaron Douglas Harriet Tubman , 1931 Sold for $14.48 million (Estimate: $2.5 million–$3.5 million Sotheby’s Works by Douglas rarely appear at auction. Measuring six feet wide, his painting Harriet Tubman (1931) portrays the abolitionist who helped enslaved African Americans escape to freedom. Commissioned by philanthropist Alfred K. Stern for Bennett College in Greensboro, North Carolina, the painting spent the past two decades on loan to the North Carolina Museum of Art. The historically Black women’s college consigned the work, with proceeds set to support the institution’s future growth, including its Women’s Health Initiative, which aims to address healthcare disparities and advance health equity for women. In the 1920s, Douglas moved from Kansas to New York, where he became a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance . The painting depicts Tubman breaking a chain above a group of onlookers, in a composition reminiscent of Eugène Delacroix ’s Liberty Leading the People (1830). Douglas described Tubman as “a heroic leader breaking the shackles of bondage and pressing on toward a new day.” Harriet Tubman sold for $14.48 million, far exceeding its $3.5 million high estimate. The result shattered Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set by Building More Stately Mansions (1944) at Swann Galleries New York in 2008. Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem Hercules and Achelous , 1590 Sold for $13.9 million (Estimate: $12 million–$18 million) Christie’s Nearly two decades after setting Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem ’s auction record, Hercules and Achelous (1590) has broken its own record. Among the Dutch Mannerist painter’s largest and most ambitious works, the painting depicts Hercules wrestling the river god Achelous, a scene drawn from Book IX of Ovid’s Metamorphoses . Born in Haarlem, the Netherlands, in 1562, Cornelis became one of the city’s leading painters, known for his dramatic compositions and muscular, contorted figures. By 1590, he had received some of Haarlem’s most prestigious commissions. The exceptional scale of Hercules and Achelous , painted on a canvas assembled from three pieces of fabric, suggests it was created for a specific patron rather than the open market. One possible early owner was Jacob Rauwart, among the wealthiest art collectors in late 16th-century Amsterdam. The oil painting sold for $13.9 million at Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale, against an $18 million high estimate. The result surpassed the artist’s previous auction record of $8.11 million, set by the same painting at Christie’s New York in 2008. Wifredo Lam Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l'herbe des dieux), 1943 Sold for $11.6 million (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million) Christie’s Painted following Wifredo Lam ’s return to Cuba in 1941, Ogue Orisa (1943) reflects the artist’s growing engagement with his Afro-Caribbean heritage. Having encountered Surrealism through Picasso and André Breton in Paris, Lam developed a distinctive visual language combining European modernism with Afro-Cuban spirituality. In Ogue Orisa , a hybrid figure emerges among sugarcane stalks and tobacco leaves, its elongated body and doubled, mask-like head reflecting the artist’s exploration of metamorphosis and identity. The painting was included in “Wifredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream,” which opened at MoMA in November 2025, where it was credited to prominent collectors Clarissa and Edgar Bronfman Jr. The retrospective was the first in the United States to survey the full trajectory of Lam’s career, highlighting his contributions to modernism and the influence of Afro-Caribbean culture on his practice. The sellers purchased the work for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1997. The painting returned to auction at Christie’s New York this week, selling for $11.6 million against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Lam’s previous auction record of $9.6 million, achieved for OMI OBINI (1943) at Sotheby’s New York in 2020. Jonas Wood Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars , 2020 Sold for $6.32 million (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million) Sotheby’s Wood, who is based in Los Angeles, brings his signature flattened perspective and densely layered patterns to the traditional landscape genre in Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars (2020). The painting transforms the carefully cultivated terrain of a Japanese garden into an intricate arrangement of shapes, textures, and saturated colors beneath a star-speckled sky. Best known for his depictions of domestic interiors, houseplants, and ceramics, Wood regularly exhibits with galleries including David Zwirner , Karma , and David Kordansky. Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars was acquired from Gagosian in 2020. The work sold for $6.83 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $5 million high estimate and narrowly surpassing Wood’s previous auction record of $6.51 million, set by Two Tables with Floral Pattern (2013) at Christie’s New York in May 2021. Fernando Botero Horse , 2006 Sold for $5.2 million. (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million) Christie’s While living in New York in the 1960s, Botero first turned his attention from painting to sculpture. “I wanted to do sculpture in bronze, but I really couldn’t afford it at that point,” he recalled. Following his move to Paris in 1973, growing international recognition enabled him to pursue the medium in earnest. The Colombian artist became known for his distinctive, rounded figures, a signature style that extended across painting and sculpture. After decades of experimenting with equine forms, Botero created Horse (2006), combining exaggerated proportions with balance and monumentality. His fascination with horses stemmed from his childhood in Medellín, where they were integral to daily life. One of an edition of three, this particular sculpture made its public exhibition debut in 2007, when it was displayed prominently beneath Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In October, Opera Gallery presented the late artist’s first solo exhibition in London in over a decade. At Christie’s this week, Horse (2006) sold for $5.2 million, narrowly surpassing Botero’s previous auction record of $5.1 million, achieved for his 1979 painting The Musicians at Christie’s New York in 2023, just two months after the artist’s death. The previous auction high for one of Botero’s bronze sculptures was $4.9 million, achieved for a different, marginally smaller sculpture also titled Horse (1992) at Sotheby’s New York in 2024. Hans Bellmer Jointure de boules (La Poupée) , 1934-1936 Sold for $1.7 million (Estimate: $1.5 million–$2.5 million) Christie’s One of only two surviving original sculptural variants of Hans Bellmer ’s celebrated doll constructions, Jointure de boules (La Poupée) (1934–36) is among the rarest works by the German Surrealist to appear at auction. Combining painting, sculpture, and assemblage, the unique relief belongs to the body of work that came to define Bellmer’s career. The other surviving sculptural variant is held in the collection of the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Bellmer began creating his unsettling, fragmented dolls in Berlin in 1933, partly in response to the Nazis’ rise to power. Photographs of his first doll, published in his 1934 book La Poupée , caught the attention of André Breton and the Parisian Surrealists. At their invitation, Bellmer created Jointure de boules (La Poupée) for the landmark “Exposition surréaliste d’objets” at Galerie Charles Ratton in Paris in 1936, the first exhibition devoted to the Surrealist object. Held in the same collection since 2000, the work sold for $1.7 million at Christie’s New York this week, against a high estimate of $2.5 million. It marked the first time a Bellmer work had surpassed $1 million at auction, exceeding his previous record of $942,000, achieved for the 1959 oil painting Les Bas rayés at Sotheby’s New York in 2025. Firelei Báez Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) , 2023 Sold for $1.32 million (Estimate: $600,000–$800,000) Sotheby’s Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez set a new auction record with Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) (2023), a large-scale painting that draws on the history of European colonialism in the Caribbean. The work depicts a brightly colored, hybrid figure with feathered limbs and a flower-like head, painted over an enlarged section of Le Jeu du Monde , a geographical game published by French cartographer Pierre Du Val in 1645. The painting was included in Báez’s first European solo exhibition, “Trust Memory over History,” presented at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark and Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg in Germany between 2023 and 2024. Born in the Dominican Republic in 1981 and now based in New York, Báez joined Hauser & Wirth ’s roster in 2023. She has since held two exhibitions with the gallery, including a 2026 New York show during the city’s May art week. Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) sold for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $800,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Báez’s previous auction record of $1.11 million, set by Untitled (Colonization in America, Visual History Wall Map, Prepared by Civic Education Service) (2021) at Christie’s New York in November 2025. Jim Nutt Loom , 1999 Sold for $1.1 million (Estimate $250,000–$350,000) Christie’s A painting that famed patron Agnes Gund once described as “my Mona Lisa” has set a new auction record for Chicago Imagist Jim Nutt . Loom (1999), a small-scale portrait of an anonymous woman with exaggerated facial features, was a highlight of the philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art trustee’s collection. Gund acquired the work from Chicago’s Karen Lennox Gallery in 2000. A founding member of The Hairy Who , the Chicago artist collective that emerged in the 1960s, Nutt initially became known for his unconventional depictions of the human figure. By the late 1980s, he had turned his attention to portraits of women, often featuring distorted proportions and unusual facial features. Working with small brushes and thinned acrylic paint, Nutt can spend up to a year on a single painting. Loom was included in his 2011 retrospective, “Coming Into Character,” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Loom sold for $1.1 million at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $350,000 high estimate. The result exceeded Nutt’s previous auction record of $966,094, set by Tooth at Bukowskis Stockholm in 2022. The painting was part of a sale of works from Gund’s collection benefiting the Gund Art Foundation, which realized $25.7 million in total. Antonio Santín Trampolín , 2025 Sold for $486,400 (Estimate: $100,000–$150,000) Christie’s Spanish artist Antonio Santín creates remarkably lifelike paintings of ornamental carpets entirely from oil paint. He applies tens of thousands of fine threads and dots using syringes powered by an air compressor, before shaping them with brushes and needles. His Trampolín (2025), a nearly 8-foot-tall painting in cobalt blue and ivory, captures the texture and folds of a woven rug in such detail that it could easily be mistaken for the real thing. Trained as a sculptor in Madrid and Athens, Santín began painting carpets in 2011 after photographing a model concealed beneath a rug in her apartment. The experiment inspired a series of paintings in which carpets appear to bulge and fold, suggesting the presence of something underneath. In more recent works, including Trampolín , Santín has moved away from reproducing existing rugs and instead invents his own patterns. The artist is scheduled to present a solo exhibition with Marc Straus in New York in 2027. Trampolín sold for $486,400 at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $150,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Santín’s previous auction record of $324,000, set by Sonora (2022) at Sotheby’s in 2024. Julia Jo One Fell Swoop , 2026 Sold for $409,600 (Estimate: $30,000–$50,000) Christie’s Brooklyn-based artist Julia Jo ’s new auction record came at the close of Christie’s evening auction. Her large-scale abstract painting One Fell Swoop (2026), created earlier this year, was the final lot of the sale. Measuring 70 square inches, the work was donated to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, a New York nonprofit founded in 1981. Born in Seoul in 1991, Jo grew up between South Korea and the United States before earning her MFA from Parsons in 2019. Her paintings begin with figures drawn directly in oil, often depicting moments of intimacy or conflict, which she gradually obscures beneath layers of color. In recent works, she has incorporated oil sticks and pastels, building compositions in which traces of the human body remain visible within the abstraction. Represented by Charles Moffett in New York and Ronchini in London, Jo was featured in Artsy’s 5 Artists on Our Radar in May 2025. One Fell Swoop sold for $409,600 at Christie’s New York, more than eight times its $50,000 high estimate. The result topped Jo’s previous auction record of $203,200, set by Rhyme or Reason (2022) at Christie’s New York in 2025. Tomma Abts Hebo , 2013 Sold for $281,600 (Estimate: $180,000–$250,000) Sotheby’s German-born artist Abts has worked almost exclusively with the same small canvas dimensions, approximately 20 by 15 inches, since 1998. Hebo (2013) follows this format, combining scarlet, coral, and amber tones in a tightly composed geometric abstraction. The painting was included in the Turner Prize winner’s 2018–19 solo exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago , her first solo museum exhibition of paintings in the United States in a decade. Working without preparatory sketches, Abts builds her compositions intuitively, layering arcs, polygons, and stripes to create an illusion of depth and movement. Represented by David Zwirner since 2005, her work is held in major collections including MoMA and Tate. Hebo sold for $281,600 at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $250,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Abts’s previous auction record of $278,671, set at Sotheby’s London in 2018. Alvaro Barrington Musician, beat of their own drum , 2021 Sold for $129,000 (Estimate: $40,000–$60,000) Phillips Multidisciplinary artist Alvaro Barrington has set a new auction record with Musician, beat of their own drum (2021), a work that reflects his interest in the connections between Caribbean culture, migration, and artistic expression. Born in Venezuela to Grenadian and Haitian parents and raised between the Caribbean and New York, Barrington draws on his upbringing to explore questions of identity, community, and belonging. Although he considers himself primarily a painter, Barrington works across a range of media. Musician, beat of their own drum , for example, combines yarn, acrylic, locks, a drum, and chains on burlap, housed in a frame made by the artist. This fall, Barrington has also presented work with High Line Art in New York, alongside his first solo exhibition on the African continent at Limbo Museum in Accra , which runs through February 1, 2027. The exhibition features paintings, sculptures, and site-specific installations made in collaboration with local artisans and fabricators. Musician, beat of their own drum sold for $129,000 at Phillips, more than doubling its $60,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Barrington’s previous auction record of $89,361, set by Black Power (2021) at Christie’s London in 2025. Irene Rice Pereira Painting in Three Planes , 1945 Sold for $128,000 (Estimate: $20,000–$30,000) Sotheby’s American abstract artist Irene Rice Pereira set a new auction record with Painting in Three Planes (1945), a box assemblage made with oil and porcelain fluid on glass and Masonite. The work was offered from the collection of Vicki and David Cox in Sotheby’s Modern Day Auction in New York. Born in Massachusetts in 1902, Pereira studied at the Art Students League in New York, where she was introduced to Cubism and Constructivism . A leading advocate of Bauhaus ideas in the United States, she helped establish the Design Laboratory in 1935, a school that encouraged experimentation with industrial materials and modern design. By the late 1930s, she had turned toward geometric abstraction, incorporating glass, plastic, and metallic pigments to explore the effects of light and transparency. She later worked at the Museum of Non-Objective Painting (now the Guggenheim Museum ) as a museum assistant, and participated in Peggy Guggenheim’s landmark “31 Women” exhibition in 1943. Painting in Three Planes sold for $128,000 at Sotheby’s New York, more than four times its $30,000 high estimate. The result topped Pereira’s previous auction record of $100,000, set by Untitled (Squares) (1944) at Capsule Gallery Auction in New York in 2021. Sofía Bassi Quijote triunfante , 1973 Sold for $121,600 (Estimate: $25,000–$35,000) Sotheby’s Mexican Surrealist Sofía Bassi ’s new auction record came with Quijote triunfante (1973), amid growing interest in her work. The result follows her first European solo exhibition, “Floating Between Earth and Sky,” at Pippy Houldsworth Gallery in London, which ran through November 14. The exhibition introduced European audiences to an artist who, despite her associations with fellow Mexican Surrealists Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo , has remained relatively little known outside her home country. Born in 1913, Bassi began painting in her fifties. Her work took a darker turn during her imprisonment in Acapulco between 1968 and 1972, after she pleaded guilty to the murder of her son-in-law. Interest in her work has also grown in Mexico this year, with Mexico City’s Georgina Pounds Gallery mounting a major exhibition of her paintings in the spring. Quijote triunfante sold for $121,600 at Sotheby’s New York, more than tripling its $35,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Bassi’s previous auction record of 800,000 Mexican pesos (approximately $46,000), set by Muñeca Reina (1974) at Morton Subastas in Mexico in May 2026. Marc Sijan Seated Security Guard , 2007 Sold for (Estimate: $15,000–$20,000) Bonhams Serbian-American sculptor Marc Sijan is known for his hyperrealistic depictions of everyday people. Seated Security Guard (2007) is part of a series of lifelike figures that have frequently commanded some of his highest prices at auction. The sculpture was acquired directly from the artist in 2008. Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in 1946 to a family of Serbian descent, Sijan creates his sculptures using plaster molds taken from live models, which he casts in polyester resin. He then applies layers of oil paint and varnish to reproduce the appearance of human skin, paying close attention to details such as wrinkles, veins, and facial expressions. His work is held in collections including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art , the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Milwaukee Art Museum . The 56-inch-tall sculpture sold for $108,200 at Bonhams, more than five times its $20,000 high estimate. The result broke Sijan’s previous auction record of $69,850, set by Standing Security Guard (2013) at Phillips New York in 2025. While his security guard sculptures have fetched his highest prices at auction, figures depicting butlers and bathers have also featured among his top sales. Hugo McCloud Untitled , 2014 Sold for $92,880 (Estimate: $30,000–$40,000) Bonhams Brooklyn-based artist Hugo McCloud is known for creating large-scale abstract paintings using unconventional industrial materials. His To Be Titled (2014) is made from aluminum foil, aluminum coating, and oil on tar paper. Born in Palo Alto, California, in 1980, McCloud is self-taught and has a background in industrial design. His practice explores themes of labor, class, and the relationship between people and their surroundings, incorporating materials ranging from tar and metal to discarded plastic bags. Represented by Sean Kelly in New York, McCloud currently has a solo exhibition, “to everything there is a season,” at the Memorial Art Gallery in Rochester, New York, on view through January 3, 2027. To Be Titled sold for $92,880 at Phillips’s Modern & Contemporary Art auction, more than doubling its $40,000 high estimate. The result broke McCloud’s previous auction record of $77,400, set by Untitled (2015) at Phillips in New York in 2026.

title: The 5 Best Booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026
summary: Against a backdrop of uncertainty in the Middle East—particularly surrounding the volatile Iran conflict—the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi opened with a noticeably robust security presence. Inside the art fair venue, Manarat Al Saadiyat, however, the mood was decidedly upbeat. Collectors, curators, and art enthusiasts filled the aisles during the VIP preview, bringing a lively energy to a fair making a defiant debut at a complicated moment for the region. Taking place from November 19th to 22nd, the fair marks a new chapter for Abu Dhabi’s art scene . Frieze announced late last year that it would take over Abu Dhabi Art , which launched in 2009 and, over 17 editions, grew into one of the region’s leading art fairs. Now organized in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism, the event brings together 89 exhibitors from 37 countries, combining international heavyweights with established and emerging galleries from across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. It is a noticeably smaller affair than last year’s Abu Dhabi Art , which featured 142 galleries, suggesting a more tightly focused approach under Frieze’s stewardship. Its arrival comes at a particularly crowded point in the international art calendar. Frieze London and Art Basel Paris in October were followed by major fairs in cities from Turin , to Mumbai, to Shanghai , to Tokyo. In that context, the pressure is on for fairs to offer something genuinely distinctive. “We have so many fairs around the world. The fair calendar is just unbelievable,” art advisor Diane Abela told Artsy. “The aim, I think, of Frieze Abu Dhabi is to create a unique platform and a unique fair.” And there is a sense that the timing is right for Abu Dhabi. The cultural ambitions that have been taking shape on Saadiyat Island—where the fair is based—for years are increasingly coming to fruition. The Louvre Abu Dhabi , which opened in 2017, has since been joined by the Zayed National Museum, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and teamLab Phenomena , while the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is scheduled to open on December 11th. What was once a bold vision for a cultural district is now, quite literally, taking shape in stone, steel, and glass. For Frieze, the challenge is to make the most of this momentum while carving out a place in an already packed calendar. Judging by the energy of its opening day, it has made a promising start. Here are five standout booths from the inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi. Taymour Grahne Projects Booth G1 With works by Ala Younis Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects ’ intimate solo booth of works by Jordanian artist Ala Younis was among the busiest at the fair during its opening hours. Featured in the curated Global Futures section dedicated to artists that engage with the histories of the U.A.E., the presentation comprises intricate mosaics from Younis’s ongoing “Climate Conditions” series. These works pay tribute to Abu Dhabi’s modernist apartment blocks and office buildings from the 1970s and ’80s, and visitors could be seen pointing to individual works, recognizing the buildings depicted in them. Trained as an architect, Younis lived in Abu Dhabi for several years and became fascinated by how these buildings were designed to withstand the region’s extreme climate. Works depict tiled façades, recessed windows, and shaded balconies, and are painstakingly composed of hand-cut stone mosaics. It’s a tactile and poignant way to depict these otherwise unassuming structures, preserving a part of the city’s architectural history amid its rapid development. As gallery founder Taymour Grahne explained, mosaic is “a way to sort of monumentalize these older buildings in the city of Abu Dhabi,” using a medium that can endure for centuries. The works are offered in editions of two, priced at $18,000 each, with an additional artist’s proof. Grahne reported strong sales during the fair’s opening, with first editions selling out and second editions also finding buyers, which included several U.A.E.-based collectors. Thompson Istanbul’s Galerist brings together four generations of women artists for a vibrant presentation exploring identity, memory, and self-representation. Framed by striking terra-cotta red walls, the booth reflects the gallery’s 25th-anniversary exhibition program, which has been dedicated entirely to solo presentations by women artists. At its center is Margaret R. Thompson ’s large triptych Firmament’s Gate (2026), a richly layered composition incorporating oil paint, earth, mica, volcanic rock dust, and turmeric. Gallery director Müge Tümen Çubukçu explained that the New Mexico–based artist developed the work for an exhibition in Istanbul, where she drew inspiration from the city’s layered history, collecting water from the Bosphorus and spices from local markets as part of her research. The resulting composition is filled with swirling, otherworldly forms that evoke spirituality and the unconscious. Nearby, sculptural ceramic vessels by Turkish artist Elif Uras draw on ancient Mesopotamian tear bottles, traditionally associated with women mourning absent or deceased husbands. Their intricate, mottled surfaces reflect the artist’s longstanding engagement with decorative traditions and what Çubukçu described as “the idea of invisible female labor in society.” The presentation also features works by two pioneering Turkish artists. A triptych of İpek Duben ’s “Şerife” paintings depicts headless, figureless garments that explore women’s social status and repression, alongside 1980s self-portraits. Meanwhile, celebrated late opera singer and painter Semiha Berksoy is represented by three works spanning more than four decades, including the expressive portraits Behice Siyavuşoğlu (1957) and Hayrünissa Binzet (1960). Works across the booth are priced between €10,000 ($10,992) and €400,000 ($439,704). A sprawling black mural of twisting, organic forms stretches across the walls, cutting through delicate ink drawings and colorful figurative paintings, while a lumpy white sculpture occupies the center of the space. Together, the works explore the complexities of migration, cultural identity, and motherhood through the lens of Filipino folklore. Central to Santos’s practice is the aswang , a shape-shifting creature from Philippine mythology traditionally associated with fear and witchcraft. As Devan Patel, co-founder of the Toronto- and Montreal-based gallery, explained, the artist is “reclaiming that figure” through a feminist perspective informed by motherhood and the natural world. Her hybrid figures, often depicted with multiple limbs and bodies resembling petrified wood, intertwine with depictions of flora native to the Philippines, reflecting the layered identity that results from diasporic experience. In the painting shroud in-situ (terno with kapa-kapa) (2026), a three-armed figure wears a traditional Philippine dress adorned with the endangered kapa-kapa flower. Elsewhere, shroud in-situ (akapulko inflorescence) (2026) features a crouching figure sprouting candlebush flowers, a medicinal plant introduced to the Philippines through colonial trade routes. Two paintings are further distinguished by elaborate wooden frames, handmade by Santos and her partner, Yarko, incorporating brass and freshwater pearls. Works on paper are priced at $4,000, while paintings range from $15,000 to $25,000.
